newsitem.title: UK: Most Britons wants currency option kept open - poll.
newsitem.headline: Most Britons wants currency option kept open - poll.

text.p: Pro-European politicians in Britain's main parties on Monday hailed a poll showing a clear majority of Britons wanting to keep open the option of joining a single European currency.
They said it proved that those members of the ruling Conservative party who have urged the government to rule out abandoning the pound sterling were fighting against the tide of public opinion.
The poll, for the European Movement, did show however that a clear majority of people basically opposed the idea of British participation in European Monetary Union (EMU).
Some 54 percent of those questioned were either generally or strongly opposed to Britain giving up the pound, with only 37 percent expressing support for the idea.
Of the 959 people polled by the MORI organisation, only 30 percent want the government to rule out joining the single currency now, while 60 percent favour keeping the option open.
Some 81 percent thought the government should publish detailed information setting out the advantages and disadvantages of the European single currency before deciding whether to join.

"The British people are voting for the future and the last thing they want is for any government, particularly a Tory government, to cut us off from the future," said Edwina Currie, a Conservative vice-chairwoman of the European Movement.
Prime Minister John Major has repeatedly rebuffed demands by so-called "Eurosceptics" to pledge never to join the European single currency, saying Britain will keep its options open.
On Monday, Eddie George, governor of the Bank of England, said he backed Major's stance in refusing to rule out joining EMU, which could be brought in as early as 1999.

Describing the idea as a "huge opportunity" for Britain's financial community, he said in an interview with the Financial Times: "I think the potential pluses are very considerable in relation to the potential minuses."
Giles Radice, the Labour member of parliament who chairs the European Movement, noted that half the people questioned in the poll said their knowledge of EU affairs was poor or fairly poor.
"I am amazed there is so much support for a single currency given that people are so ignorant about it," he said.
